examples.t: Ten emails, each with a **spam score** (suspicious words, 0 to 10). Someone has checked every email and recorded whether it **really is spam**, so we have the true answers.

two-classes.t: Each email belongs to one of **two classes**: not spam (**label 0**) or spam (**label 1**). That is **binary classification**. The 0 and 1 are names, not amounts.

feature-input.t: A new email arrives. Its feature is the **spam score, 7.5**. The classifier will look at it and **choose a class**.

classifier.t: Our simple classifier applies a rule: **score at least 4 means spam**, otherwise not spam. Later lessons show how such rules are built from data.

prediction.t: The score **7.5 is at least 4**, so the predicted class is **spam (1)**.

compare-label.t: We also know the **true class** of this email: spam (1). A prediction is **correct when the predicted class equals the true class**.

correct-example.t: **Predicted spam, actually spam:** correct. The classifier's output and the true label agree.

wrong-example.t: Another email has score **4.5**. The rule says spam, but it is **real mail (0)**. Predicted and true class differ, so this prediction is **incorrect**.

binary-task.t: Features go in, a **predicted class** comes out, and we compare it with the **true class**. On our ten emails this rule is right **8 times and wrong twice**.
